answer.evidence: The crossbeam (rows 9-18) has an outline at row 9, then a light tan top band at rows 11-12 with rivets, and darker brown front-face rows 13-17 that shade into a dark base at row 18. That makes a short top of about 3 rows over a front face of about 5-6 rows. Each post is 14 px wide and has a cap at rows 5-9 with a light tan top plane and a darker lower edge, above a vertical front face running to row 46. The cap is not an ellipse, and the front-edge line is weak. The open gate leaves (rows 19-45) are drawn as flat corrugated panels beside the opening. The post caps and beam top are small (3-4 rows), but they are present and sit above a tall front face, so this reads as three_quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are fine: 12 visible tones per tile (references 12 and 10), 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines are tinted (dark brown beside wood, dark blue-grey beside metal) rather than sticker black. By eye, though, the piece is thinner and flatter than the house references. The posts and crossbeam read as about 3-4 wood steps, with little grain and no per-plank or knot dots. The corrugated gate leaves are narrow slivers with only a few steps and a small rust accent, and they show no real ridge-by-ridge highlighting. The whole piece has 19 distinct colours against 66 and 185 in the references. It is a sparse object, so I did not judge it on tile density alone. Still, a careful artist would likely see it as shallower than the Beodeul tile roofs and stone walls, with fewer shading steps (about 4 against 5-6) and less surface texture. When in doubt, fail.

answer.evidence: Each post has a lighter cap block at rows 4-8, about 14 px wide against the narrower post below, ending in a dark edge at row 9. styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts are at reference level: 12 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 0% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outline is tinted dark brown or blue-grey and not a black sticker line. By eye the piece is still thinner than the references. The whole gateway uses only 19 colours across wood, metal and rust, so each material gets about 3-4 steps against Beodeul's 5-6. The posts and crossbeam read as a base brown with one highlight edge and a dark side. The corrugated leaves are mostly two-tone vertical ribs with a few rust dots. There are no per-plank grain dots, no stone-by-stone shading and no per-tile highlights like the reference roofs and walls. It is clean and tinted, not flat, but next to the dense references it looks flatter and simpler. I'm failing it on the shallow ramps and sparse grain, not on its size.

answer.evidence: The posts (the tallest volume) end in caps at rows 4-8, with a light diagonal-shaded top plane over 4-5 rows and the post face below from row 9 to 46. The crossbeam (rows 9-17) has a darker back row 10, then a light tan band with bolts at rows 11-12 that acts as the front-edge line, then a gradient front face at rows 13-17 with a red plate and dark shadow at rows 17-18. So the beam top is about 3 rows. The gate leaves at rows 19-45 are corrugated vertical panels with no top edge line, so they have no visible top surface. The posts and beam do show tops over a front face of 3+ rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a thin, sparse prop, so I judged it by eye as well as by the numbers. It matches the references on the primary facts: 12 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 0% near-flat coverage like both references, and 0% neutral dark edge pixels, so the outlines are tinted. The outlines read as dark brown beside the wood posts and beam, and dark blue-grey beside the metal leaves. There is no uniform black sticker line, and some forms separate by value alone. The posts show about 4 steps (cap highlight, light, mid, dark). The corrugated leaves show a few ribs with rust or red accents and no large single-colour areas. It has fewer steps than the roughly 5-6 per material in the references, and its total palette is small (19 colours against 185 and 66), but that is consistent with a locked palette. A careful artist would accept it next to the references as slightly simpler, but not as a flat sticker.
